title: Improvising together, counting time and the flute
summary: Zanco defines Dixieland as simultaneous solos, listens to others' solos, cannot count time, and once rented a flute and taught himself.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Well, do you think the guys listen to each other while they're playing?

Um, I do. I don't know. I guess most everybody does. But, uh, when, uh, either a trombone or a clarinet will take a solo. Well, I sit there and I really listen to it and I enjoy what I hear, you know.

Well, now you say, last Sunday when I was there, I heard you play something, a lick, and then I heard Archie adapt part of that, you know, into his lick right after that, you know. But just some little variation on the tune, you know, and he worked that right into his, just answered you, you know. Yeah. Like, you know, it's obvious the guys in the band, all together, even though they're all playing solo.

Well, I think, uh, if you play as a group long enough, you almost know what the other guy's thinking. And you can do that same thing, say, uh, follow him, uh, maybe take the lead, you know, work at the guys first, or like that. Uh, most, uh, well, I don't know, uh, not being, uh, a reading musician, or really knowing that much about music. I would think that while one guy is playing a solo, a regular musician would be counting time. See, he knows how many beats have to go in a measure, and he knows when this other guy's solo is just ready to end, see. Now, with me, it's not like that. I don't know how to count time. So I just, you know, I come in when I think the solo is over, we see. Like, when one guy's playing a solo, I think he's finished, and I'll come in. I might be wrong on that now, but I've always had that impression that while one fellow's playing a solo, a regular musician is counting the timing. You know, keeping time, or counting how many measures. Well, some many men do that during the symphony, but... Well, uh, they'll show me a sheet of music. I'm lucky I can read the name of the tune, much less the notes on it.
You didn't study music in school at all.
No, no, no. Well, I made a statement. Huh? Pardon me?
Didn't you tell me one time that you played the flute once?

Well, uh, I didn't take lessons. I had a flute. And, uh, at the time, I was listening to, uh, well, a lot of classical music. And I heard something, I said, boy, I'd like to know how to play this. So I had this flute. I rented a flute. And I learned how to play, uh, all the walls of the flowers and some of the stuff from Pete and the Wolf. Uh, I can't think of the names of it. But anyway, I just like the sound, so I'll play. Well, that's the same thing I do with the trumpet. I like the sound, and I'll play it, see? I mean, if I went and bought this trumpet, and if I didn't learn how to play it, I was just out of money, you see? So, it was either play or die, you know? So I learned how to play it.
